title: Overcoming the Incentive Collapse Paradox
one_liner: When AI does the work, paying people by accuracy fails—so audit them instead to force effort at fixed cost.
lead: In AI-assisted work, a human and a machine collaborate: the human checks or refines the machine's output, but their effort is hidden. Paying by accuracy seems natural, yet it breaks catastrophically—as the AI gets better, the human needs more and more money to stay motivated, eventually requiring infinite payment. This paper solves that by switching from payment-by-accuracy to payment-by-detection: randomly audit the human's work and pay based on whether they were truly trying.

paras: Imagine a company uses AI to tag photographs. A person reviews each tag before it ships: does the AI's label make sense? The person's work is effortless when the AI is bad (they catch obvious mistakes easily) but becomes grueling when the AI is already very good (spotting the rare remaining errors takes focus). Yet the company wants to pay fairly: it offers money proportional to correctness—more correct output, more pay.

This creates a trap. When the AI is bad, the human catches most errors and both the work and pay feel reasonable. But as the AI improves, two things happen: (1) the work becomes harder (fewer obvious mistakes to catch means more careful focus needed), and (2) the pay per correct output stays the same or shrinks (because the AI's contribution grows). The person becomes unmotivated and stops trying. To fix this, the company raises the pay per correct tag—but this never ends. As AI accuracy approaches human-level, the human needs infinite payment to stay engaged at all. This is the incentive collapse paradox.

callout.b: The core problem in one sentence.
callout.html: Paying by accuracy creates a perverse incentive: the better the AI, the less humans try (because catching rare errors is effortful, and the pay per correct output shrinks as AI improves), and the more you must pay to keep them engaged—with no upper limit.

panels.title: 1. AI is bad, humans work hard
panels.caption: AI makes blunders. Humans catch them easily. Work is clear, money feels earned.

panels.title: 2. AI improves, humans slacken
panels.caption: Mistakes vanish. Finding rare errors is tedious. Why try hard when it's already correct?

panels.title: 3. Company raises pay desperately
panels.caption: To keep the human engaged, company doubles and redoubles the pay per correct tag.

panels.title: 4. Random audits replace accuracy pay
panels.caption: Pivot: pay a fixed amount, but randomly sample work. Caught slacking incurs penalty.

panels.title: 5. Effort stays high at bounded cost
panels.caption: Human keeps working at steady effort because detection is always a risk, regardless of AI quality.

steps.text: Accuracy-based payment breaks as AI improves (humans need infinite pay because the pay-per-mistake shrinks while the effort-to-catch-one rises), so humans need infinite pay to stay motivated.
Randomly sample and grade the human's real effort, independent of task difficulty or AI accuracy.
Fix the base pay; dock it if audits reveal shirking. The human knows they might be caught.
Choose how often to sample (5%? 10%?) to balance cost of audits against the effort you need.
Spend your audit budget wisely: focus audits on harder tasks where slacking is most tempting.

paras: The paper changes the payment rule from accuracy-based to auditing-based. Instead of paying proportional to how correct the final output is, it pays a fixed amount and randomly audits the work, penalizing insufficient effort. The human's incentive shifts from a direct link to output quality (which collapses) to a detection-avoidance motive (which stays constant).

hidden.h2: What the paper measures: effort level
hidden.name: Human effort level
paras: The hidden quantity is the human's actual effort—how hard they are trying on each task. It is not directly visible; you observe only the output they produce and what the AI says. Effort can be high (careful review, thoughtful corrections) or low (rubber-stamping the AI, guessing, skipping careful checks).

The paper estimates effort by auditing: when sampled, an auditor carefully grades whether the human actually tried, independent of whether the final answer was correct. An auditor can tell if a tag was reviewed with care or rubber-stamped, even if both happen to be correct.

heat.caption: Darker cells show effort indicators and how audits detect shirking; highlight marks the payment mechanism's elements.

reads.html: The human's effort is their attention, focus, and care applied to each review. High effort means the AI's output is scrutinized; low effort means it passes through unchecked. Effort lives in the human's mind and hands, not in the data.

The paper models effort as a strategic choice by a rational agent—humans choose their effort level given the incentive structure (pay + audit risk). An audit reveals effort by measuring whether the human's review process and corrections align with a high-effort strategy.

mechanism.h2: How auditing forces effort at finite cost
paras: When you pay by accuracy alone, the human faces a math problem: as AI accuracy climbs, the marginal benefit of their effort (catching one more rare mistake) shrinks to zero, so they stop trying. Raising the payment does not solve this—it just creates a race to the top with no finish line.

Auditing breaks this trap by rewiring the incentive. When the human knows they are randomly sampled (say, 5% of their work), the cost of being caught shirking (a penalty or job loss) becomes a constant threat, independent of AI quality. Whether the AI is 90% or 99% accurate, the human faces the same detection risk. This makes sustained effort rational because the expected loss from an audit (probability of being caught times the penalty) stays constant regardless of AI accuracy, while shirking remains risky.

The paper formulates this precisely: design an audit rate (how often to sample) and an audit budget (how much auditing costs), then prove that you can enforce strictly positive, controllable human effort at a cost that stays finite even as AI accuracy approaches perfection. Audits measure effort directly, not accuracy indirectly, so they sidestep the collapse entirely—human motivation no longer depends on task difficulty or AI quality.

stages.s: Human effort level (high or low, unobserved)
Human reviews AI output, produces corrections
Random sample: audit selected outputs to grade effort
Compare effort observed to minimum threshold
Pay base amount, dock penalty if shirking detected

math.words: Total cost is the fixed payment plus the audit cost times audit rate, plus the expected penalty if audit finds low effort.
math.equation: total_cost = base_pay + audit_cost * audit_rate + penalty * prob_caught_low_effort
symbols: Cost to inspect one sample (auditor time)
Fraction of work actually sampled (e.g., 0.05 for 5%)
Docked pay if caught not trying (or termination cost)
Probability effort is below minimum given current payment

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose base_pay = $50 per task, audit_cost = $10 to inspect one output, audit_rate = 5% (sample 1 in 20).
Penalty for caught shirking = $200 (job loss risk / docked pay).
If human effort is low (prob_caught = 0.8), then:
Expected penalty = $200 * 0.8 = $160 (amortized per undetected task, weighted by risk)
Key: the base pay is fixed at $50, independent of AI accuracy. The human stays motivated because the audit risk ($160 * 5% = $8 expected loss per task if lazy) outweighs the temptation to slack.

math.note: As AI accuracy rises, the accuracy-based payment would spike to infinity, but this formula stays constant—the human's effort is no longer tied to task difficulty.

charts.title: Accuracy-based payment (fails)
charts.note: As AI improves, required payment explodes because humans stop trying without infinite incentive.

charts.title: Auditing-based payment (this paper)
charts.note: Payment stays flat because effort is enforced by audit risk, not accuracy. The human's motivation no longer depends on task difficulty.

items.html: If auditing costs almost nothing, you will audit often, but the overhead adds up. If detected shirking has no real penalty (easy to rehire), humans still slack because the expected loss is negligible.
If auditing is very costly (hard to assess true effort), you audit rarely, giving the human many undetected chances to slack. The mechanism breaks if the audit budget runs out.
If it is unclear what counts as genuine effort (some tasks are inherently harder to review), auditors may disagree on whether the human tried, leading to inconsistent penalties and eroding trust.

With a credible audit (cheap enough to sample often, consistent in grading), a fixed penalty (clear to the human), and clear effort thresholds (audit looks for verifiable review steps), the mechanism holds: humans stay motivated and the company pays a predictable, finite amount regardless of AI quality.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A demo should simulate a hiring task (or image-labeling, or document-review) where an AI system completes most of it and a human refines it. Set up a fixed payment for the human, then sweep the audit rate (0%, 1%, 5%, 10%, 20%) and track: (1) the human's observed effort level, (2) the total cost (payment + audits + penalties), and (3) the final task accuracy. Show that as you increase audit rate, human effort rises and levels off at a steady, positive level (because the detection risk discourages shirking), while total cost stays bounded (audits are expensive but limited by the rate you choose). Compare this to an accuracy-based payment scheme (without audits) and show that accuracy-based payment requires unbounded increases to sustain effort as AI accuracy improves (because the pay-per-error collapses as AI gets better).
demo.metric_eq: total_cost = base_pay * num_tasks + audit_cost * (num_tasks * audit_rate) + penalty * (num_caught_shirking)
demo.closing: The demo must make impossible to miss: auditing enforces effort at finite cost (because the audit mechanism measures effort directly rather than inferring it from accuracy), while accuracy-based payment fails catastrophically as AI gets better (because the marginal benefit of human effort shrinks as AI improves).
